slides.label: Route
slides.notes: Open by framing the lecture as implementation work, not a catalogue of products. The nonlinear operations in this chapter are reliable only when the lower product kernels expose signs, metric contractions, grade filters, and sparse accumulation. Preview the route from basis-mask multiplication to structure tests, then to inverses, factorization, delta products, and meet/join algorithms.

slides.label: Coordinate Kernel
slides.notes: Use this slide to separate representation from computation. Students may hear dense array and imagine dense algebra, but the product loops should still walk only occupied coordinates. Emphasize that nonlinear routines reuse this kernel repeatedly, so a small sign, grade, or metric mistake here becomes a false inverse, false blade, or wrong meet later.

slides.label: Geometric Product
slides.notes: Work through the displayed example slowly. The useful habit is to separate three decisions: count swaps for sign, contract repeated basis vectors through the metric, and accumulate into the mask produced by exclusive-or. This is the engine underneath the versor scalar check, the generic inverse matrix, and the delta product grade selection.

slides.label: Outer And Inner Products
slides.notes: Make the grade filter the main idea. The outer product is not a separate mysterious multiplication; it is the geometric product with the grade that represents span growth. The inner product keeps contraction grades after the metric has acted. The delta product used later is another grade filter, but it chooses the highest nonzero grade.

slides.label: Inversion
slides.notes: Contrast the two inverses as engineering choices. A versor inverse is cheap because the object is already a product of invertible vectors, so the reverse recovers the inverse up to one scalar. The general multivector inverse is valuable as a fallback and comparison, but it should report conditioning and identity error rather than pretending to be equally stable.

slides.label: Elementary Functions
slides.notes: This slide prevents the lecture from making inverse, meet, and join feel like the only nonlinear operations. The same design rule applies to exponentials: if the square is scalar, choose the closed form; otherwise scale the input, evaluate a bounded series, and square back. Logarithms are presented as specialized families rather than a solved general problem.

slides.label: Classification
slides.notes: Stress that classification is not a cosmetic label for display. The implementation must know whether fast inverse formulas and geometric transformations are legitimate. A uniform-grade test alone is tempting and wrong, so the algorithm first checks inverse behavior and the grade-one action on vectors before deciding whether the surviving object is a blade or a more general versor.

slides.label: Blade Factorization
slides.notes: Explain why factorization is a recovery problem. The coordinate array has lost the explicit list of vectors, but meet, join, and geometric display often need those vectors back. The largest-coordinate basis blade gives stable candidates in the source algorithm, while the notebook nullspace view makes the same subspace condition inspectable through the equation x wedge B equals zero.

slides.label: Negative Tests
slides.notes: Use the e12 plus e34 example as a guardrail against shallow implementations. It passes the pure-grade test, but it is not one oriented two-plane, so a factor list would be misleading. The right behavior is a controlled rejection with a residual or exception that tells downstream meet, join, and display routines not to proceed.

slides.label: Delta Product
slides.notes: Connect this slide back to the grade-filter discussion. The delta product does not require first factoring both blades; the geometric product naturally contracts shared factors, and the highest remaining grade records what is unshared. Once that grade is known, the meet and join grades follow before we construct either object.

slides.label: Meet And Join
slides.notes: Walk students through the loop as a paired search. A candidate factor either has a projection that belongs in the common part, or a rejection that helps remove directions outside the join. The practical point is that the routine is allowed to stop early when one target grade is reached, then compute the companion product from the meet or join relation.

slides.label: Robustness
slides.notes: Use this as the implementation realism slide. Symbolic geometry says two subspaces either share a factor or they do not. Floating point geometry says the decision depends on scale, noise, and tolerance. The threshold plot should make clear why tests around nearly coincident planes are more informative than tests that only use exact coordinate axes.

slides.label: Sparse Accumulation
slides.notes: This slide is a bridge from mathematical formulas to debuggable code. When a nonlinear routine fails, the error often entered through a product bucket much earlier. Encourage logging or table-driven tests that show masks, signs, contractions, and grade filters for representative collisions, because those records make meet and inverse bugs far easier to localize.

slides.label: Test Cases
slides.notes: Close the technical development with tests because tests are how these algorithms become trustworthy. The table deliberately starts below the nonlinear layer: product signs, contractions, and grade filters must be correct before higher operations can be interpreted. Then it climbs through inverse, factorization, classifier, meet/join, and threshold cases, matching the notebook's sanity-check philosophy.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: End by giving students a debugging ritual rather than a memory dump. When a nonlinear product looks wrong, ask which structure the implementation claimed to recognize and what evidence supported that claim. The best routines expose product-kernel records, inverse residuals, factorization residuals, delta grade predictions, and threshold decisions, so failures become diagnosable instead of opaque.
